questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The Qur'an was revealed to Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W) over a period of approximately
questions.explanation: The revelation of the Qur'an spanned about 23 years, beginning in Makkah and continuing after the migration to Madinah.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The angel through whom the Qur'an was revealed to Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W) was
questions.explanation: Angel Jibril (Gabriel) served as the channel of revelation, delivering the words of the Qur'an to the Prophet.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The first revelation received by Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W) occurred in the cave of
questions.explanation: The Prophet received his first revelation in the Cave of Hira, located on Jabal an-Nur near Makkah.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The first word revealed to Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W), commanding him to read/recite, was
questions.explanation: The very first revealed word was 'Iqra', an instruction to read or recite, marking the beginning of the Qur'an's revelation.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The first Caliph credited with initiating the formal compilation of the Qur'an into a single collected text was
questions.explanation: Abu Bakr ordered the compilation of the Qur'an into one manuscript after many reciters (huffaz) died in the Battle of Yamama.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The Caliph responsible for standardising the Qur'anic text into a single authoritative version and distributing copies to major cities was
questions.explanation: Uthman standardised the Qur'anic text to prevent regional variations in recitation, sending official copies to key Islamic centres.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The chapter of the Qur'an regarded as its opening and recited in every unit of the five daily prayers is
questions.explanation: Suratul-Fatihah, the 'Opening', is the first chapter of the Qur'an and is recited in every rak'ah of the daily prayers.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The Surah that describes the story of the Abyssinian army and elephants that attacked the Kaaba is
questions.explanation: Suratul-Fil (The Elephant) recounts how Allah destroyed the army of Abraha, which had attempted to attack the Kaaba using elephants.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The short Surah revealed to affirm the absolute oneness of Allah, rejecting any partners or equals, is
questions.explanation: Suratul-Ikhlas concisely declares the pure oneness (Tawhid) of Allah, stating that He neither begets nor is begotten.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The Surah that instructs the believer to declare disassociation from disbelief and the worship of false gods is
questions.explanation: Suratul-Kafirun ('The Disbelievers') declares a clear distinction between the worship of Allah and the worship practices of disbelievers.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The Surah announcing 'the Night of Decree', regarded as better than a thousand months, is
questions.explanation: Suratul-Qadr describes Laylatul-Qadr (the Night of Decree/Power), a night of immense spiritual significance during Ramadan.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The Surah in which Allah reassures the Prophet that He has neither forsaken nor become displeased with him is
questions.explanation: Suratud-Duha ('The Morning Brightness') was revealed to comfort the Prophet during a pause in revelation, reassuring him of Allah's continued favour.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The Surah that speaks of Allah's help and victory, and instructs glorifying and seeking Allah's forgiveness, is
questions.explanation: Suratun-Nasr ('The Help') refers to the coming of Allah's victory and instructs the believer to glorify and seek forgiveness from Allah.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The Surah traditionally understood as containing the first verses revealed to the Prophet is
questions.explanation: Suratul-Alaq begins with the command 'Iqra' (Read), and its opening verses are traditionally regarded as the very first revelation.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The verse widely known as 'Ayatul-Kursi' (the Throne Verse), praised for describing Allah's majesty and knowledge, is found in
questions.explanation: Ayatul-Kursi is verse 255 of Suratul-Baqarah, celebrated for its powerful description of Allah's sovereignty, knowledge, and eternal nature.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The final chapter of the Qur'an, seeking Allah's protection from the whisperings of Satan, is
questions.explanation: Suratun-Nas ('Mankind') is the very last chapter of the Qur'an, seeking Allah's protection from the evil whisperings that afflict people.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The set of rules governing the correct pronunciation and articulation of Qur'anic recitation is called
questions.explanation: Tajwid comprises the rules ensuring accurate and proper pronunciation of Arabic letters and words when reciting the Qur'an.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The Tajwid rule concerning the pronunciation of a 'Noon Sakinah' (a silent noon) when followed by certain letters is important for correctly applying
options: rules such as Idgham, Ikhfa, Iqlab, and Izhar
questions.explanation: Noon Sakinah rules in Tajwid determine how a silent noon is pronounced depending on the following letter, including Idgham, Ikhfa, Iqlab, and Izhar.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The Tajwid rule concerning prolongation of certain vowel sounds during recitation is called
questions.explanation: Madd rules govern how long certain vowel sounds should be elongated when reciting specific letters in the Qur'an.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The nasal sound produced when pronouncing noon or meem with a shaddah, or under certain Tajwid rules, is called
questions.explanation: Ghunnah refers to the nasal resonance applied when pronouncing noon or meem in specific contexts during Qur'anic recitation.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The Qur'an is divided for ease of recitation and study into thirty equal parts known as
questions.explanation: The Qur'an is divided into thirty Ajza (singular: Juz), commonly used to complete a full recitation over the month of Ramadan.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The complete recitation of the entire Qur'an from beginning to end is referred to as a
questions.explanation: A Khatm refers to the completion of reciting the entire Qur'an, often undertaken as a spiritual practice, especially during Ramadan.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: A scholarly explanation or commentary that interprets the meaning of Qur'anic verses is called
questions.explanation: Tafsir refers to the discipline and literature dedicated to explaining and interpreting the meanings of the Qur'an's verses.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: A brief stopping point in Qur'anic recitation, observed to take a breath or pause appropriately, is guided by rules known as
questions.explanation: Waqf rules in Tajwid indicate where a reciter may appropriately pause during recitation without distorting the intended meaning.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The 'echoing' or bouncing sound produced when certain strongly articulated letters occur with a sukun (vowel-less state) is called
questions.explanation: Qalqalah describes the distinctive echoing sound applied to specific letters when they carry a sukun, adding clarity and correctness to recitation.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: A Hadith is best defined as
options: a ruling made by a modern Islamic scholar
a historical account written by non-Muslims
a verse directly revealed in the Qur'an
a saying, action, or approval attributed to Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W)
questions.explanation: Hadith refers to the recorded sayings, actions, and tacit approvals of the Prophet, forming a key source of Islamic guidance alongside the Qur'an.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The Sunnah refers to
options: the legal code of pre-Islamic Arabia
only the verses of the Qur'an
the practices, habits, and way of life exemplified by Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W)
the rulings made exclusively by the four Caliphs
questions.explanation: Sunnah encompasses the Prophet's practical example, including his habits, conduct, and approach to life, which Muslims are encouraged to follow.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The chain of narrators through which a Hadith has been transmitted is called the
questions.explanation: Isnad refers to the chain of transmission, listing each narrator who passed the Hadith down, used to assess its authenticity.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The actual text or content of a Hadith, containing the words or description of the Prophet's action, is called the
questions.explanation: Matn is the substantive text of a Hadith, distinct from the Isnad, which is the chain of narrators verifying its transmission.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The collection of Hadith regarded as the most authentic and reliable, comprising six major books, is known as
questions.explanation: Sihah al-Sittah refers to the six most trusted Hadith collections, compiled by scholars who rigorously verified each report's authenticity.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Among the six authentic Hadith collections, the two most highly regarded by Muslim scholars are
options: Sunan Abu Dawud and Sunan Ibn Majah
Muwatta Imam Malik and Musnad Ahmad
questions.explanation: Sahih Al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim are widely regarded as the most authentic Hadith collections due to their rigorous authentication standards.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The first Hadith in An-Nawawi's collection, famously beginning 'Actions are judged by intentions', emphasises the importance of
options: sincerity of intention (Niyyah) in all deeds
questions.explanation: The famous Hadith on intentions teaches that the value and reward of an action depend fundamentally on the sincerity of the intention behind it.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Among An-Nawawi's forty Hadiths, several address the Pillars of Islam and the Articles of Faith (Iman) mainly to teach
options: rules of trade and commerce alone
the biographies of the Umayyad Caliphs
the foundational beliefs and practices that define a Muslim's faith and worship
questions.explanation: These Hadiths outline the core pillars of practice and belief central to being a Muslim, forming the foundation of Islamic religious life.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Several Hadiths in the prescribed collection teach that a Muslim should show kindness to
options: only those who can repay the kindness
only wealthy members of the community
neighbours, regardless of their faith or background
only fellow Muslims within their own family
questions.explanation: The Prophet strongly emphasised kindness and good treatment of neighbours as an essential part of good character in Islam.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Hadiths concerning cleanliness commonly teach that cleanliness is
questions.explanation: A well-known Hadith states that cleanliness is half of faith, underscoring its spiritual as well as physical importance in Islam.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Hadiths that address 'forbidden acts' (Muharramat) generally instruct Muslims to
options: engage freely in any action without restriction
avoid actions and behaviours that Allah and His Prophet have prohibited
follow only local customs regardless of religious guidance
prioritise personal preference over Islamic teaching
questions.explanation: Teachings on forbidden acts guide Muslims to steer clear of behaviours explicitly prohibited in Islamic law and Prophetic teaching.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: A Hadith is generally classified as 'Sahih' (authentic) when its chain of narrators is found to be
options: broken at multiple points with unknown narrators
narrated by only one unreliable individual
unbroken, and each narrator trustworthy and precise in memory
passed down without any chain of narration at all
questions.explanation: Scholars classify a Hadith as Sahih (authentic) when it has a continuous, verifiable chain of trustworthy and accurate narrators, along with a sound text.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: A Hadith Qudsi is distinct from an ordinary Prophetic Hadith mainly because its meaning is attributed to
options: one of the Prophet's companions only
Allah Himself, though expressed in the Prophet's own words
questions.explanation: A Hadith Qudsi conveys a divine message from Allah, but unlike the Qur'an, it is phrased in the Prophet's own wording rather than being a direct scriptural revelation.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Imam Al-Bukhari is especially renowned among Hadith scholars for his
options: role as one of the four Rightly Guided Caliphs
collection of only weak and unreliable narrations
extremely rigorous standards in verifying the authenticity of each Hadith he included
authorship of the Qur'an's commentary alone
questions.explanation: Imam Al-Bukhari applied exceptionally strict criteria when authenticating Hadiths, contributing to his collection's status as the most trusted in Islam.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: A Hadith among An-Nawawi's collection teaching that 'None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself' emphasises
options: the obligation of the Hajj pilgrimage
empathy, brotherhood, and selflessness among believers
questions.explanation: This well-known Hadith highlights the importance of genuine empathy and goodwill toward fellow believers as a mark of true faith.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: A Hadith teaching that 'the strong believer is better... than the weak believer' while both remain good is generally understood to encourage
options: pride and arrogance over other believers
rejection of anyone perceived as physically weak
physical strength alone, without regard for character
striving for strength of character, effort, and capability while maintaining humility
questions.explanation: This Hadith encourages believers to strive for strength (in faith, effort, and capability) while still valuing goodness in every believer regardless of ability.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Hadiths concerning manners (Adab) commonly teach Muslims to
options: avoid greeting anyone outside their immediate family
greet others with peace (Salam), speak kindly, and show good conduct in daily interactions
ignore the feelings of others in social settings
questions.explanation: Hadiths on manners place strong emphasis on good conduct in everyday life, including greeting others warmly and speaking with kindness.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The Hadith stating 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should speak good or remain silent' teaches Muslims to
options: speak as much as possible regardless of content
remain permanently silent at all times
be mindful of their speech, avoiding harmful or idle talk
questions.explanation: This Hadith encourages believers to carefully consider their words, choosing to speak only what is good or otherwise to stay silent.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: A Hadith teaching that 'Paradise lies at the feet of mothers' is generally understood to emphasise
options: the requirement to perform Hajj through one's mother
the great honour and duty of kindness owed to one's mother
the superiority of fathers over mothers
a literal geographic location of Paradise
questions.explanation: This widely cited Hadith underscores the immense respect, kindness, and duty of care that children, especially sons, owe to their mothers.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The study of Hadith terminology and classification (such as Sahih, Hasan, and Da'if) is part of the broader discipline known as
questions.explanation: Mustalah al-Hadith is the specialised field of scholarship dedicated to classifying and evaluating the authenticity of Hadith reports.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Tawhid, the foundational concept of Islamic monotheism, refers to
options: belief in the absolute oneness and uniqueness of Allah
belief in multiple gods with Allah as the chief deity
belief that prophets should be worshipped alongside Allah
belief that angels share Allah's divine power
questions.explanation: Tawhid is the core Islamic doctrine affirming that Allah alone is God, with no partners, equals, or associates in His divinity.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The dimension of Tawhid affirming that Allah alone is the Creator, Sustainer, and Controller of the universe is called
questions.explanation: Tawhid ar-Rububiyyah affirms Allah's sole authority over creation, sustenance, and governance of the universe.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The dimension of Tawhid affirming that worship must be directed to Allah alone, without any partners, is called
questions.explanation: Tawhid al-Uluhiyyah requires that all acts of worship, such as prayer and supplication, be directed exclusively to Allah.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The dimension of Tawhid affirming Allah's unique names and attributes, as He has described Himself, without distortion or comparison, is called
questions.explanation: This dimension affirms Allah's unique names and attributes exactly as revealed, without human distortion, denial, or comparison to created beings.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Shirk, one of the gravest sins in Islam, refers to
options: fasting during the month of Ramadan
associating partners with Allah in His lordship, worship, or attributes
questions.explanation: Shirk is the sin of ascribing partners or equals to Allah, directly violating the principle of Tawhid.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Major shirk (Shirk al-Akbar) refers to acts such as
options: worshipping idols or other deities alongside or instead of Allah
minor acts of showing off in good deeds
small lapses in sincerity during worship
questions.explanation: Major shirk involves outright directing worship to something or someone other than Allah, which is considered to nullify one's faith.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Minor shirk (Shirk al-Asghar), while less severe than major shirk, still poses a serious spiritual danger and includes acts such as
options: performing good deeds to be seen and praised by others (Riya)
denying the existence of Allah entirely
questions.explanation: Riya (showing off in worship or good deeds) is a commonly cited example of minor shirk, undermining sincerity even while outwardly appearing pious.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The Articles of Faith (Iman) in Islam include belief in Allah, His Angels, His Books, His Prophets, the Last Day, and
questions.explanation: The six Articles of Faith conclude with belief in Al-Qadar, Allah's foreordained decree governing all that happens.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Belief in Allah's Angels, as part of the Articles of Faith, includes accepting that angels
options: are created beings who carry out Allah's commands without disobedience
can be seen by all people at will
are equal partners with Allah in divinity
are simply symbolic figures with no real existence
questions.explanation: Muslims believe angels are obedient beings created by Allah specifically to carry out His commands, without free will to disobey.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Belief in Allah's Books, as an Article of Faith, includes accepting scriptures such as
options: the Torah, Psalms, Gospel, and the Qur'an as the final revelation
books written by Islamic scholars after the Prophet's death
only the Qur'an, with no earlier scriptures
questions.explanation: Muslims believe in earlier revealed scriptures (Torah, Psalms, Gospel) while regarding the Qur'an as the final, complete, and unaltered revelation.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Taharah, an important concept in Fiqh, refers to
options: ritual and physical cleanliness required for acts of worship
questions.explanation: Taharah encompasses the rules of cleanliness, both physical and ritual, necessary before performing acts of worship such as prayer.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The ritual washing performed before the five daily prayers, involving washing the face, hands, and feet, is called
questions.explanation: Wudu is the minor ritual ablution performed before prayer, involving washing specific parts of the body in a prescribed order.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The full ritual bath required after major impurity, such as after sexual intercourse, is called
questions.explanation: Ghusl is the complete ritual washing of the entire body, required to remove major ritual impurity before worship.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The dry ablution performed using clean sand or dust, when water is unavailable or its use is harmful, is called
questions.explanation: Tayammum permits ritual purification using clean earth or sand as a substitute for water when water is unavailable or its use would cause harm.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The obligatory five daily prayers observed by Muslims are collectively known as
questions.explanation: Salat refers to the five daily obligatory prayers that form one of the central pillars of Islamic worship.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The special congregational prayer performed by Muslims on Friday afternoons, replacing the Zuhr prayer, is called
questions.explanation: Jumu'ah is the obligatory Friday congregational prayer for Muslim men, including a sermon (khutbah), replacing the regular Zuhr prayer.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The special prayer performed to mark the two major Islamic festivals, Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, is called
questions.explanation: Eid prayers are special congregational prayers performed on the mornings of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha to celebrate these festivals.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The funeral prayer performed for a deceased Muslim, involving no bowing or prostration, is called
questions.explanation: Janazah is the special funeral prayer offered collectively for a deceased Muslim, distinct in form from the regular daily prayers.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Zakat, the compulsory almsgiving pillar of Islam, is generally calculated as a set percentage of a Muslim's
options: total income regardless of any threshold
inherited property alone, excluding cash savings
qualifying wealth held above a minimum threshold (nisab) for a full lunar year
questions.explanation: Zakat is calculated on qualifying wealth that meets or exceeds the nisab (minimum threshold) and has been held for a full lunar year, typically at a rate of 2.5%.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Zakat funds are specifically intended to be distributed to categories such as
options: the poor, the needy, and other eligible recipients specified in the Qur'an
any purpose the payer personally prefers
only the wealthy members of society
questions.explanation: The Qur'an (Surah At-Tawbah 9:60) specifies particular categories of eligible recipients for Zakat, including the poor, the needy, and other defined groups.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Sawm, the obligatory fasting observed during the month of Ramadan, involves abstaining from food, drink, and other prescribed acts from
questions.explanation: Muslims observing Sawm during Ramadan abstain from eating, drinking, and other specific acts from the break of dawn until sunset each day.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Among those exempted from fasting during Ramadan, with an obligation to make up missed days later, are
options: healthy adults with no valid excuse
questions.explanation: Islam provides exemptions from fasting for those who are sick or travelling, with an obligation to make up the missed days once able.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Hajj, the pilgrimage to Makkah, is obligatory upon every adult Muslim who
options: is physically and financially able to undertake the journey
has performed Umrah at least once before
is above the age of sixty
questions.explanation: Hajj is required once in a lifetime for every adult Muslim who has the physical capability and financial means to perform it.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: A central rite of Hajj involves circling the Kaaba seven times, known as
questions.explanation: Tawaf is the ritual of circumambulating the Kaaba seven times, a core rite performed during both Hajj and Umrah.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Another key rite of Hajj involves walking or running seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwah, known as
questions.explanation: Sa'i commemorates Hajar's search for water for her son Isma'il, and involves pilgrims moving between the hills of Safa and Marwah seven times.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The standing (vigil) at the plain of Arafah, considered the most essential rite of Hajj, is called
questions.explanation: Wuquf at Arafah is regarded as the most essential pillar of Hajj; a pilgrimage without this standing is considered invalid.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Shariah is best described as
options: the comprehensive body of Islamic law derived from divine sources
a set of local customs with no religious basis
a single book written by early Islamic scholars
a term referring only to criminal punishments
questions.explanation: Shariah encompasses the full body of Islamic law governing worship, ethics, and social conduct, drawn from foundational Islamic sources.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The primary sources of Shariah, in order of authority, are generally identified as
options: only the Qur'an, with no other sources recognised
the personal opinions of any individual scholar
the Qur'an, the Sunnah, Ijma (consensus), and Qiyas (analogical reasoning)
questions.explanation: Islamic jurisprudence draws primarily from the Qur'an and Sunnah, supplemented by scholarly consensus (Ijma) and analogical reasoning (Qiyas) where needed.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Ijma, as a source of Islamic law, refers to
options: the consensus of qualified Islamic scholars on a particular legal matter
a ruling made unilaterally by one ruler
a verse taken directly from the Qur'an
a Hadith narrated by a single companion
questions.explanation: Ijma represents the collective agreement of qualified scholars on an issue not explicitly addressed in the Qur'an or Sunnah.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Qiyas, as a source of Islamic law, refers to
options: the personal preference of a single judge
a ruling based purely on local custom
direct quotation from the Qur'an alone
reasoning by analogy to extend a known ruling to a new, similar situation
questions.explanation: Qiyas involves applying the reasoning behind an existing ruling to a new case that shares similar underlying circumstances.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The period in Arabian history before the advent of Islam, characterised by ignorance and widespread idol worship, is called
questions.explanation: Jahiliyyah describes the pre-Islamic period in Arabia, marked by idolatry, tribalism, and various social ills that Islam later addressed.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: In the pre-Islamic era, the Arabian Peninsula's social structure was strongly organised around
questions.explanation: Pre-Islamic Arabian society was fragmented into tribes, with loyalty and identity centred primarily around kinship and clan ties.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: A significant social practice condemned by Islam that was prevalent during the Jahiliyyah era was
questions.explanation: The practice of burying infant daughters alive, driven by social prejudice against girls, was a grave injustice that Islam explicitly condemned and abolished.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W) was born in the city of
questions.explanation: Prophet Muhammad was born in Makkah, a city that was already an important trading and religious centre in Arabia.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W) received his first revelation and call to prophethood at approximately the age of
questions.explanation: The Prophet received his first revelation in the Cave of Hira at around the age of forty, marking the beginning of his prophetic mission.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: In the early years of his prophetic mission in Makkah, Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W) and his followers faced
options: immediate widespread acceptance by all Makkans
intense persecution from the Makkan tribal leaders
official government protection from the start
questions.explanation: The Prophet and early Muslims endured significant persecution and hostility from Makkah's ruling tribal elite, who felt threatened by his message.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The migration of Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W) and his followers from Makkah to Madinah is known as the
questions.explanation: The Hijrah, the migration from Makkah to Madinah in 622 CE, marks a pivotal turning point in Islamic history and the start of the Islamic calendar.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Following the Hijrah, Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W) established in Madinah what is often described as
options: a temporary settlement with no lasting structure
the first organised Islamic state, uniting diverse tribes and faith communities
a purely military camp with no civil administration
questions.explanation: In Madinah, the Prophet built a structured community and governance system, including the Constitution of Madinah, uniting Muslims and other groups under agreed terms.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The first major battle between the Muslims of Madinah and the Makkan forces, resulting in a decisive Muslim victory despite being outnumbered, was the Battle of
questions.explanation: The Battle of Badr in 624 CE was a significant early victory for the small Muslim force against a much larger Makkan army.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The battle in which the Muslims suffered a setback partly due to some archers leaving their assigned positions was the Battle of
questions.explanation: At the Battle of Uhud, a strategic setback occurred when a group of archers left their post prematurely, allowing the Makkan cavalry to counterattack.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The battle in which the Muslims of Madinah successfully defended the city by digging a trench around it, on the advice of Salman al-Farisi, was the Battle of
questions.explanation: The Battle of the Trench (Khandaq) saw Muslims successfully repel a large confederate siege of Madinah by digging a defensive trench around the city.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The peace agreement made between the Muslims and the Makkans, initially seen by some as unfavourable to the Muslims but later regarded as a strategic victory, was the
questions.explanation: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah established a truce between Muslims and Makkans, ultimately allowing Islam to spread more peacefully in the following years.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The largely peaceful takeover of Makkah by the Muslims, resulting in the destruction of idols in the Kaaba, is known as
questions.explanation: The Conquest of Makkah in 630 CE was achieved with minimal bloodshed, leading to the removal of idols from the Kaaba and mass conversions to Islam.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The final sermon delivered by Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W) toward the end of his life, summarising key principles of Islamic conduct and equality, is called the
questions.explanation: The Farewell Sermon, delivered during his final pilgrimage, emphasised themes of human equality, justice, and the completion of his prophetic mission.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The first Caliph to lead the Muslim community after the death of Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W) was
questions.explanation: Abu Bakr, a close companion of the Prophet, was chosen as the first Caliph, guiding the community through the challenges immediately following the Prophet's death.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: During Abu Bakr's caliphate, a major internal challenge he addressed was
options: the standardisation of the Qur'anic text
the Wars of Apostasy (Riddah) against tribes who rejected Islamic authority
a war against the Byzantine Empire alone
questions.explanation: Abu Bakr's caliphate focused significantly on suppressing rebellions from tribes who renounced allegiance to Islam and refused to pay Zakat after the Prophet's death.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The second Caliph, known for major territorial expansion and significant administrative reforms such as establishing the Islamic calendar, was
questions.explanation: Umar ibn al-Khattab oversaw substantial territorial expansion and introduced key administrative reforms, including the Hijri calendar.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The third Caliph, notable for compiling and standardising the official text of the Qur'an, was
questions.explanation: Uthman ibn Affan's caliphate is especially remembered for the standardisation and distribution of the official Qur'anic text.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The fourth Caliph, a close relative and companion of the Prophet, whose caliphate faced significant internal political conflict, was
questions.explanation: Ali ibn Abi Talib's caliphate was marked by internal strife, including conflicts that contributed to significant divisions within the early Muslim community.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The four Caliphs who succeeded Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W) directly are collectively known as
questions.explanation: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali are together known as the Rightly Guided Caliphs, revered for their close association with the Prophet and their leadership.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Islam was introduced to West Africa mainly through
options: Muslim traders and scholars travelling the trans-Saharan trade routes
direct military conquest by Arabian armies
the arrival of Ottoman naval forces
questions.explanation: Islam spread into West Africa gradually and largely peacefully, carried by Muslim merchants and scholars engaged in trans-Saharan trade.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Among the West African empires significantly influenced by the spread of Islam were
questions.explanation: Islam had a profound influence on the Mali, Songhai, and Kanem-Bornu empires, shaping their governance, scholarship, and trade connections.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The spread of Islam in West Africa contributed significantly to the growth of centres of Islamic learning, such as
questions.explanation: Timbuktu became a renowned centre for Islamic scholarship in West Africa, home to institutions such as the Sankore mosque and university.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: Muslim traders and scholars in West Africa played a role beyond religious teaching by also contributing to
options: the destruction of all existing West African political institutions
the abolition of trade in the region
the spread of literacy, legal systems, and administrative practices influenced by Islamic scholarship
the introduction of European colonial administration
questions.explanation: Beyond religion, the spread of Islam brought Arabic literacy, Islamic legal thought, and administrative practices that influenced governance in West African empires.

questions.subject: Islamic Studies
questions.text: The general approach through which Islam spread across much of West Africa is best described as
options: imposed solely by European colonial powers
gradual and largely peaceful, primarily via trade and scholarship
immediate and entirely through armed conquest
questions.explanation: Unlike some regions where Islam spread rapidly through conquest, its introduction to West Africa was generally a gradual process rooted in trade relationships and scholarly influence.
